newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordics on EMU track but membership doubtful.
newsitem.headline: Nordics on EMU track but membership doubtful.

text.p: The European Union's three Nordic members are well on track to meet key criteria for joining economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 but the Scandinavian involvement in the single currency remains in doubt.
Political rather than economic factors may determine when and if Sweden and Denmark enter EMU. Finland, on the other hand, seems determined to take part in the first wave.

The European Commission's forecasts published on Wednesday suggested that all three would have public deficits below three percent of gross domestic product in 1997, the key year for qualifying for EMU, as well as in 1998.
Denmark was even forecast to show a budget surplus of 0.3 percent of GDP in both years, the only EU country other than Luxembourg to boast budget figures in the black.

In addition, their debt/GDP ratios would continue to decline in both years, even though Finland was the only Nordic country where the level was forecast at below 60 percent of GDP, the target ceiling set by the EU's Maastricht treaty.
Apart from the key deficit and debt criteria, countries need to meet EMU requirements on inflation, interest rates and currency stability to qualify for the single currency.
The latter could pose a problem for Sweden, were it to seek membership, as it remains outside the EU's exchange rate mechanism, which groups 12 of the bloc's 15 currencies.

Despite the improving Nordic performance in terms of meeting the single currency criteria, however, only Finland seems clearly committed to join EMU in 1999, although its parliament will not take the final decision until early 1998.
Economist Wike Groenenberg at Salomon Brothers in London said that meeting the criteria was not really the issue for the Nordics but rather the political desire to participate.
"Of the three Nordics in the EU it is Finland which has shown the biggest commitment to EMU," she said, adding that there was much less enthusiasm in Denmark and Sweden.
Finnish Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto reiterated on Tuesday that his country meets all EMU criteria and aims to be in monetary union from the start.
In contrast, Denmark has already opted out from monetary union and a new referendum would be needed to allow the country to join.
Danish Economy Minister Marianne Jelved has made clear this is unlikely any time soon, at least not before the planned EMU start in 1999.
Neighbouring Sweden, which like Finland joined the EU in 1995, has not yet decided whether to take part, saying its parliament will decide the issue in October or November.
Finance Minister Erik Asbrink is due to announce the position of the leadership of the ruling Social Democrats in mid-May.
There is a widespread belief among market analysts and political observers that the ruling Social Democrats, split on the issue, would decide to wait on EMU membership.
"I expect that Sweden won't join (in 1999)," said European economist Stephanie Pfeifer at Deutsche Bank Research.
The uncertainty about the Nordics' participation in EMU is reflected in surveys based on financial prices monitored by U.S. investment firm JP Morgan.
According to its "EMU calculator" published this week, the probability of Sweden joining in 1999 was 59 percent and 44 percent for Denmark.
But the figure for Finland was 77 percent, putting the likelihood of it joining higher than for countries such as Ireland, Spain and Portugal.
